directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Sauvignon Blanc is vigorous and productive but benefits from canopy management to control its naturally sprawling growth. One of the world's most popular white wine grapes, it produces small, thick-skinned green grapes prized for wines with pronounced herbaceous, citrus, and 'green' aromatic character that vary noticeably by growing region and ripeness at harvest, from grassy and tart in cool climates to tropical and riper in warmer ones. Vigorous and adaptable to a range of soils and climates, it is one of the more forgiving wine grapes for a home vineyard, tolerating moderate disease pressure better than some of its more delicate relatives. Prune to control the vine's vigorous, sprawling growth habit, thin leaves around fruit clusters to promote airflow and even ripening, and harvest based on flavor and acid balance rather than a fixed calendar date.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Syrah (called Shiraz in Australia and South Africa) is a vigorous, heat-loving variety well suited to warm growing regions.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Syrah (called Shiraz in Australia and South Africa) is a vigorous, heat-loving variety well suited to warm growing regions. This bold, deeply colored red wine grape produces small, dark-skinned berries that yield rich, full-bodied wines with dark fruit, pepper, and smoky notes, thriving in warm, sunny climates from France's Rhône Valley to Australia's Barossa Valley where it has become that country's signature red grape under the Shiraz name. Vigorous and generally reliable in warm regions, it tolerates heat well but is susceptible to bunch rot in humid conditions, making canopy management for airflow important in more humid growing areas. Train to a trellis system that supports its vigorous growth, thin fruit if overcropping to concentrate flavor, and provide full sun and warmth for the best ripening.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Malbec prefers warm, sunny conditions and is somewhat more cold-sensitive than many other red wine grapes.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Malbec prefers warm, sunny conditions and is somewhat more cold-sensitive than many other red wine grapes. Originally a minor Bordeaux blending grape in France, this deeply colored red variety found its true expression in the high-altitude vineyards of Mendoza, Argentina, where abundant sunshine and cool nights produce the rich, plush, dark-fruited wines with soft tannins that have made Malbec Argentina's signature grape and an internationally beloved red wine style. It is somewhat prone to coulure (poor fruit set in cool, wet spring weather) and benefits from a warm, sheltered site with reliable sunshine through flowering and fruit set. Provide full sun and a warm site sheltered from late spring cold snaps, prune to a moderate crop load for the best concentration, and harvest when tannins are ripe alongside sugar development.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis or head-trained system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Grenache is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant, well suited to hot, dry growing climates.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis or head-trained system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Grenache is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant, well suited to hot, dry growing climates. One of the most widely planted red wine grapes in the world, it produces high sugar levels even in scorching heat, yielding fruity, medium-to-full-bodied red wines and, when picked earlier or pressed gently, some of the world's finest dry rosés, particularly from southern France's Rhône Valley and Spain, where it is also known as Garnacha. Its thin skin and upright growth habit make it well suited to traditional bush-vine (head-trained, unstaked) cultivation in hot, arid climates, requiring minimal irrigation once its deep root system is established. Consider head-training rather than a full trellis system in very hot, dry climates for traditional bush-vine culture, and monitor sugar levels closely since it can ripen quickly and lose acidity if left too long in hot weather.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Sangiovese is a late-ripening variety that needs a long, warm growing season to fully mature.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Sangiovese is a late-ripening variety that needs a long, warm growing season to fully mature. The most widely planted red wine grape in Italy and the backbone of Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino, and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, it produces medium-bodied, high-acid, savory red wines with notes of tart cherry and dried herbs that pair especially well with food, reflecting the grape's central role in Tuscan cuisine and culture. It is a genetically variable and somewhat finicky grape, with dozens of recognized clones differing in cluster size, vigor, and quality potential, making clone selection an important consideration for a home vineyard planting. Prune to manage its naturally vigorous growth, thin fruit clusters if needed to concentrate flavor, and be prepared for a long hang time on the vine, since it ripens later than many other red varieties.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Tempranillo is an early-ripening variety, an advantage in regions with shorter growing seasons or early fall rains.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Tempranillo is an early-ripening variety, an advantage in regions with shorter growing seasons or early fall rains. Spain's noble red wine grape and the foundation of Rioja and Ribera del Duero, its name derives from the Spanish word 'temprano' (early), reflecting its tendency to ripen earlier than many other red varieties, producing medium- to full-bodied wines with notes of red fruit, leather, and tobacco that develop further complexity with oak aging. Its earlier ripening window makes it a practical choice for regions with shorter growing seasons or a risk of early autumn rain damaging late-ripening varieties still on the vine. Prune to a moderate crop load for concentrated flavor, provide full sun and good air circulation to reduce disease pressure, and take advantage of its earlier harvest window in climates where fall weather can be unpredictable.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Pinot Gris is a genetic mutation of Pinot Noir and shares that variety's preference for cooler growing climates.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Pinot Gris is a genetic mutation of Pinot Noir and shares that variety's preference for cooler growing climates. A pinkish-gray-skinned mutation of Pinot Noir, this white wine grape produces two distinctly different wine styles depending on region and winemaking approach: light, crisp, neutral wines when labeled Pinot Grigio in the Italian style, or richer, more aromatic, fuller-bodied wines when labeled Pinot Gris in the Alsatian French style. It shares much of Pinot Noir's cold hardiness and preference for cooler climates, along with a similar susceptibility to fungal disease in humid conditions, requiring attentive canopy management for airflow. Prune for an open canopy to reduce disease pressure in humid climates, and decide on harvest timing based on the intended wine style, since earlier picking favors the crisper Pinot Grigio style and later picking favors richer Pinot Gris character.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Muscat grapes are among the oldest cultivated grape varieties and are unusual for producing wines that actually smell and taste distinctly of fresh grapes.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Muscat grapes are among the oldest cultivated grape varieties and are unusual for producing wines that actually smell and taste distinctly of fresh grapes. One of the oldest and most widespread grape families in the world, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains is prized for its intensely floral, distinctly grapey aroma, unusual among wine grapes for producing wine that actually smells and tastes like fresh table grapes, used to make everything from light, lightly sparkling Moscato d'Asti to sweet fortified dessert wines. The grapes are also excellent eaten fresh off the vine, giving this variety dual value as both a wine and table grape in a home garden setting. Provide full sun and good air circulation, thin clusters if fruit set is heavy to concentrate the distinctive floral aromatics, and pick based on desired sweetness level, since Muscat can be used for both dry and sweet wine styles depending on harvest timing.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology
